belief: A good Christian never gets angry.
origins: Many of us learned that anger is always sinful, that nice people never show it, and that Christians should be calm. Where anger was explosive in the home, we may fear it in ourselves. So we bury it, and it comes out as sarcasm, withdrawal, headaches, or a sudden blowup.
teaches: Paul says, “Be angry, yet do not sin. Do not let the sun set upon your anger,” which assumes anger is not itself sin. The psalmist says, “Be angry, yet do not sin; on your bed, search your heart and be still.” Jesus “looked around at them with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart,” and He made a whip and drove the money changers out of the temple. James says, “Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger, for man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires.” Proverbs says, “A gentle answer turns away wrath.” Anger is a signal. What we do with it matters.
self_statements: Angry feelings mean I am a bad Christian.
I should never feel this way.
If I get angry, I am sinning.
I have to bury my anger.
errors: Believing anger is either absent or sinful.
Insisting that I should never feel anger.
Feeling guilty about anger and concluding that I am bad.
Burying anger, which then leaks out sideways.
questions: What was I taught about anger, and by whom?
What does my anger tell me about what I value or what hurt me?
Did Jesus ever express anger? What was its source and its limit?
What are healthy ways to express anger?
What happens when I bury it?
What can I do tonight to search my heart and be still?
truth: Anger itself is not a sin. It is a signal that something matters to me or has hurt me. I can bring it to God, express it respectfully, and not let it control me. Jesus felt anger too, and He never sinned.
hw_truths: Be angry, yet do not sin.
I can bring anger to God.
A gentle answer turns away wrath.
I can express anger without harming.
log: Each time you feel anger, write what hurt or mattered, and one healthy response.
actions: Write what you are angry about and what it protects.
Pray it out honestly, using the psalms as a model.
Walk, breathe, or journal before responding.
Share your concern respectfully with the person involved.
prayer: Lord, I have been afraid of my anger. Help me hear what it is telling me, bring it to You honestly, and respond in ways that heal rather than harm. Amen.
hw_questions: What was I taught about anger?
What is my anger telling me?
What healthy outlets do I have?
What happens when I bury it?
